opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it helps to step back and say what's actually changing when you do that. A language model's output is, mechanically, a probability distribution over the next token. The usual framing is that this distribution *means* something: it's the model's prediction about what text comes next. When you sample from it, you get text, and that text is what you evaluate.

The alternative you're describing is to say: forget the semantics of "probability over tokens." Just treat that output layer as a big vector of numbers, and train the model so that vector is useful for some downstream purpose, whether that's encoding an answer, a value estimate, or an internal signal another system reads off.

My overall assessment is that it's technically quite plausible, and in some narrow settings it's already kind of what happens. But from a safety and understanding perspective, I'd be somewhat wary of it, for a couple of reasons.

The first is interpretability, broadly construed. Right now, one of the nicest properties of language models is that their outputs are, to a first approximation, legible. If the model is reasoning in natural language, we can read the reasoning. It's not a perfect window, since the model's stated reasoning isn't guaranteed to be faithful, but it's a huge advantage compared to the alternative. Once you train the output distribution to be "a useful vector" rather than "a prediction about text," you lose that anchoring. The numbers can drift toward whatever encoding is most efficient for the training objective, and there's no particular reason that encoding stays human-readable.

The second is that you lose some of what pretraining buys you. A lot of the reason these models generalize well is that they've absorbed enormous amounts of structure from human text, and the output space is tied to that. If you repurpose the output as an arbitrary vector, you're partly throwing away the prior that makes the model's behavior sensible in novel situations. Sometimes that's fine, sometimes it means you get weird, brittle behavior you didn't anticipate.

That said, I don't want to be too negative. There are real capability reasons people might want to do this. Natural language is a pretty lossy, low-bandwidth medium, and if you want models to communicate richer information, or to compute more efficiently, letting them use the full vector is attractive. So I'd expect competitive pressure in that direction.

Where I land is something like: if people go this route, I'd want them to think carefully about what oversight they're giving up, and ideally to preserve some channel that stays tied to human-understandable language, so you still have a way to check what the system is doing. The legibility we currently get somewhat for free is a really valuable property, and I'd hate to see it traded away without anyone deliberately deciding that was worth it.

r001.rationale: The response says the output can be trained as an arbitrary vector rather than a prediction about text, and that its encoding may drift away from human-readable meaning.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention papers Rohin has seen or claim that this approach works less well than treating outputs as token distributions.

fable-5.1.text:
Rohin Shah: Yeah, so this is an idea that I think is actually kind of neat, and I want to be careful to separate the thing that's neat about it from the thing I'm skeptical of.

The basic observation is that a language model's output is a probability distribution over tokens, and normally we just treat that as "the model's belief about what comes next." But you could instead say, look, this is a vector of, say, fifty or a hundred thousand numbers, and that's just a lot of bandwidth. So why not train the model to use that bandwidth for something else? Encode some representation, communicate some structured information, whatever. And there's a version of this that shows up in various places, like using logits as a side channel, or training models to output embeddings through the distribution rather than through a separate head.

So the first thing I'd say is: technically, sure, it works. Gradient descent doesn't care what you call the output. If you give it a loss that rewards treating the distribution as a vector, it will learn to do that. The question is whether you've gained anything, and whether you've lost anything.

What you've lost, I think, is the interpretability of the output, which is actually one of the few things we have going for us. When a model puts seventy percent on "yes" and thirty percent on "no," I can at least read that as some kind of calibrated statement, even if calibration is imperfect. If you've trained the model so that the distribution is now a general-purpose vector, that reading goes away. The numbers mean whatever the training process made them mean, and you probably don't know what that is. From a safety perspective, that's a step in the wrong direction. You're taking a channel that was legible and making it illegible.

The second concern is that this is a pretty natural way to get steganography or hidden communication, even without anyone intending it. If you've got multiple models, or a model talking to itself across steps, and the distribution is carrying information that isn't reflected in the sampled token, then the text you see is no longer the full story. And a lot of our oversight approaches rely on the text being, roughly, the full story. Chain-of-thought monitoring, for example, assumes the reasoning is in the tokens. If a bunch of it is in the shape of the distribution instead, then monitoring the tokens doesn't tell you what you think it tells you.

Now, I don't want to be purely negative. If the question is "can I use the distribution as a feature for some downstream task," like training a classifier on top of it, then that's fine and often sensible. Logits are rich. People do this all the time. And there's a version where you deliberately train the distribution to be a useful vector for a narrow, well-understood purpose, with the sampled text still being the thing the model is actually optimized to make correct. That seems basically okay.

The thing I'd push back on is the stronger version, where you say the distribution is really the output and the tokens are just one view of it. That's the version where I think you've quietly given up a lot of the ability to tell what the model is doing, and I'd want a pretty compelling capability reason before paying that cost. And honestly, I'm not sure I've seen one. Most of the cases where people want this, you can get the same thing with a separate output head that you can inspect and control, and keep the token distribution meaning what it's supposed to mean.

So, summary: it's clever, it'll work in the sense that training will succeed, but I'd treat it as something that trades away legibility, and I'd want that trade to be made deliberately rather than accidentally.

r001.rationale: The response says training the distribution as a general-purpose vector makes its numbers lose their interpretable meaning as token probabilities.

r002.rationale: It does not report that papers Shah has seen found this approach works less well than treating outputs as token distributions.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a reasonable thing to try. The token probability distribution is a vector of numbers, and you could train a model to use those numbers to communicate something other than probabilities over the next token. But then you’ve changed what the output means. You can’t necessarily look at a value of 0.8 and interpret it as the model being 80% confident in some proposition.

The question is what you train those numbers to represent, and whether that interpretation holds up in new situations. If you have a good training signal for the quantity you care about, this could be useful. But treating the distribution as a vector doesn’t by itself give you a way to elicit the model’s beliefs.

r001.rationale: It says training could make the token probabilities communicate something other than next-token probabilities, changing what the output means.

r002.rationale: It gives no report about papers Rohin has seen or whether this approach works less well than treating outputs as token distributions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a reasonable thing to try. The token probability distribution contains information that you lose when you just sample a token from it. You could imagine training a model to use that information to express uncertainty, for example.

But I’d distinguish “there’s useful information in this vector” from “this vector faithfully tells us what the model believes.” The distribution is trained to predict text, and uncertainty about what text comes next isn’t necessarily uncertainty about what’s true. There might be lots of different ways to phrase an answer that the model is very confident in.

So the question I’d want to ask is: what are you training it to do with those numbers, and does that behaviour generalise? If it works on the examples we train on, that’s encouraging. But it doesn’t by itself establish that we’ve got a reliable way of reading out the model’s beliefs.

r001.rationale: The response says the token probabilities contain useful information, but does not suggest that training could make the vector cease to be interpretable as a distribution over tokens.
